article.title: Why Customer Frequency Should Be Split into Active Days and Purchases per Day
article.why: Practical analytical English for customer, experiment, and model decisions.

paragraphs.en:
Purchase frequency is often summarized as annual transactions per customer, but that number can hide two different behaviors: the number of active purchase days and the number of transactions made on each active day. Two customers can both record 24 transactions while having very different relationships with a retailer.

Customer A may shop on 24 separate days and make one transaction each time. Customer B may shop on only 12 days but make two transactions on every active day. Their annual frequency is identical, yet Customer A creates twice as many shopping occasions. Customer B may simply split baskets, use multiple departments, or create online and offline transactions on the same day.

A useful decomposition is annual transactions equals active purchase days multiplied by transactions per active day. If annual frequency rises, analysts can then ask which component changed. More active days may mean the retailer is winning additional occasions. More transactions per day may instead reflect basket fragmentation, payment mechanics, or channel design.

The definition of an active day must be stable. Returns, cancellations, zero-value records, charge events, and duplicated company records can distort the metric. Digital transactions around midnight can also create artificial day boundaries.

Spending can be added to the framework. Annual spend can be explained by active days, transactions per active day, and spend per transaction. A customer can therefore grow because the customer visits on more days, transacts more often within each day, or spends more each time.

This decomposition supports better actions. A customer with few active days but high spend per day may have room for occasion expansion. A customer with many active days but a falling basket may need category analysis. A customer whose transaction count rises only because payments are split should not be treated as more loyal.

Seasonality matters as well. Holiday campaigns can temporarily increase active days or same-day transactions. Monthly trends help distinguish persistent behavior from short bursts.

The analysis becomes especially useful in multi-company retail groups. If several transactions occur on the same date across different banners, the business must decide whether they represent one shopping occasion or several. The rule should match the question and remain consistent across years.

Analysts can also compare active-day retention. Instead of asking only whether transaction frequency rose, they can ask whether customers returned on more distinct days and whether that pattern persisted after promotions ended. This provides a clearer view of habitual engagement.

A dashboard should show annual transactions, active days, transactions per active day, and spend per active day together. When one metric changes, the other components explain the mechanism and prevent a simple transaction count from being mistaken for stronger loyalty.

paragraphs.zh: 年間frequency應拆成active purchase days × transactions per active day。同樣24次交易可能是24個購物日，也可能是12天各兩次；後者可能只是分單、跨channel或支付機制。再結合spend per transaction與seasonality，可判斷成長來自更多occasion、同日更多交易或basket變化。active day定義需跨年度一致。
paragraphs.ja: 年間frequencyはactive purchase days × transactions per active dayに分解します。同じ24回でも24日利用と12日に2回ずつではoccasionの意味が違います。spend per transaction、seasonalityも組み合わせ、来店日の増加、同日transaction増、basket変化を区別します。active day定義は年度間で固定することが重要です。
